subject: Vocabulary
topic: Medical and health-related words — mixed tiers
description: Diagnosis, prognosis, chronic, acute, benign, malignant, contagious, epidemic — exam-frequent

questions.stem: A CHRONIC illness is one that:

options.option_text: Comes on suddenly and ends in a few days at most
Persists for a long period and recurs over many years
Spreads rapidly between members of a household
Cannot be detected by any standard medical test

questions.explanation: CHRONIC = long-lasting / persistent (months to years; often life-long). Examples: diabetes, hypertension, asthma, chronic kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis. Opposite term: ACUTE — sudden onset, short duration (e.g., flu, appendicitis). Distractor 1 = acute. Distractor 3 = contagious (infectious). Distractor 4 = idiopathic / occult illness.

questions.stem: A BENIGN tumour is one that:

options.option_text: Spreads rapidly to other organs across the body
Is non-cancerous and does not invade nearby tissue
Is always fatal regardless of treatment given
Forms only in skin cells of older patients

questions.explanation: BENIGN — non-cancerous, slow-growing, well-defined boundary, doesn't invade neighbouring tissue or metastasise. Often harmless unless pressing on a vital structure (a benign brain tumour can still need removal due to space limits). Examples: lipoma, fibroma, common moles. MALIGNANT — cancerous, invasive, can metastasise. Distractor 1 = malignant behaviour. Distractor 3 = false generalisation; benign tumours are usually treatable. Distractor 4 = unrelated.

questions.stem: PROGNOSIS in a medical setting refers to:

options.option_text: Identifying the disease from its observable signs and symptoms
Predicting the likely course and outcome of the disease
Selecting the medication best suited to treat the disease
Examining the patient physically to look for any abnormality

questions.explanation: PROGNOSIS — Greek 'pro' (before) + 'gnosis' (knowledge). Doctor's prediction of how the disease will progress: how long, how serious, recovery vs deterioration, survival rate. DIAGNOSIS — identifying which disease (= Distractor 1). Distractor 3 = treatment plan / therapy. Distractor 4 = clinical examination.

questions.stem: A CONTAGIOUS disease is one that:

options.option_text: Develops only as a side-effect of medical treatment
Spreads from one person to another by direct or indirect contact
Originates from genetic mutations passed down at birth
Worsens because of an unhealthy lifestyle and poor diet

questions.explanation: CONTAGIOUS — Latin 'contagio' (contact). Spreads via direct contact, droplets, fomites, etc. Examples: COVID-19, common cold, measles, chickenpox, ringworm. INFECTIOUS — broader term for any disease caused by pathogens (some infectious diseases are not very contagious — e.g., tetanus, rabies require specific exposure). EPIDEMIC — sudden rise in cases above expected baseline in a region. PANDEMIC — epidemic across multiple countries / continents. ENDEMIC — consistently present at a baseline level (e.g., malaria in some regions). Distractor 1 = iatrogenic. Distractor 3 = hereditary / genetic. Distractor 4 = lifestyle disease.

questions.stem: A PLACEBO is best understood as:

options.option_text: A new drug that has just been approved by regulators
An inactive substance given as a control in a drug trial
A targeted antibiotic that fights only one type of bacteria
A herbal supplement sold as a daily wellness product

questions.explanation: PLACEBO — Latin 'I shall please'. Sugar pill / saline injection / inert substance with no pharmacological effect. Used as the CONTROL ARM in randomised controlled trials so the active drug's effect can be separated from psychological/observational effects. THE PLACEBO EFFECT — measurable improvement in symptoms even from inert treatment, due to expectation, conditioning, regression to the mean, and clinician attention. Distractor 1 = a new approved drug, not inert. Distractor 3 = narrow-spectrum antibiotic. Distractor 4 = nutraceutical / supplement (active ingredients claimed but unregulated).

questions.stem: An EPIDEMIC differs from a PANDEMIC in that an epidemic is:

options.option_text: Always more severe than any pandemic disease
Confined to a particular region or country, not global
Affects only a single age-group within a country
Caused only by viruses, while pandemics by bacteria

questions.explanation: EPIDEMIC — sudden rise in disease cases above the baseline in a particular region / country. PANDEMIC — an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents (a pandemic is a 'large epidemic'). The WHO declares pandemics; COVID-19 was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. ENDEMIC — disease that is always present at a baseline rate (e.g., malaria in many tropical regions). OUTBREAK — small, localised cluster of cases. Distractor 1 — severity isn't the defining factor; geographic spread is. Distractor 3 — age isn't the criterion. Distractor 4 — pathogen type isn't the criterion.

questions.stem: An ANTIBIOTIC is a medicine that primarily acts against:

options.option_text: Allergic reactions to common pollen and dust mites
Bacterial infections, by killing or inhibiting bacteria
Viral infections like influenza or the common cold
Inflammatory pain and fever from any general source

questions.explanation: ANTIBIOTICS — kill bacteria or inhibit their growth. Examples: penicillin (Fleming, 1928), amoxicillin, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin. They DO NOT work against viruses (overprescription drives antibiotic RESISTANCE — a major global-health crisis). Distractor 1 = antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine). Distractor 3 = antivirals (e.g., oseltamivir for flu); cold has no specific antiviral. Distractor 4 = anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs like ibuprofen) and antipyretics (paracetamol). Mis-classifying these is a common medical-vocabulary error.

questions.stem: PALLIATIVE care in medicine primarily aims to do which of the following?

options.option_text: relieve symptoms and improve the patient's quality of life
cure the underlying disease through targeted drug therapy
prevent the disease from spreading to other individuals
destroy the pathogen responsible for causing the illness

questions.explanation: A is correct because 'palliative' (from Latin palliare, to cloak) means providing relief from pain and distressing symptoms without curing the disease — used in terminal cancer care, for example. Option B describes curative treatment, which is the opposite intent. Options C and D describe preventive and antimicrobial actions respectively, neither of which is the goal of palliative care.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes a SYNDROME in medical terminology?

options.option_text: a group of symptoms that consistently appear and occur together
a single symptom traced to one well-identified pathogen
a drug prescribed specifically to treat one defined disease
a laboratory test used to detect the presence of a disease

questions.explanation: A is correct: a syndrome is a recognisable cluster of signs and symptoms that tend to occur together, e.g., Down Syndrome or Metabolic Syndrome. Unlike a disease, a syndrome may lack a single identified cause. Option B describes a symptom (singular), not a syndrome. Options C and D describe a prescription drug and a diagnostic test respectively — both unrelated to the term.

questions.stem: A NOSOCOMIAL infection, by medical definition, is one that is:

options.option_text: contracted during a stay or procedure in a hospital or clinic
transmitted directly from an animal to a human host
caused by a severely compromised immune system response
triggered by prolonged exposure to environmental pollutants

questions.explanation: A is correct: nosocomial comes from the Greek 'nosokomein' (to tend the sick) and refers to healthcare-associated infections — MRSA or ventilator-associated pneumonia are classic examples. Option B describes a zoonotic infection. Option C describes opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients, which may overlap but is not what nosocomial means. Option D describes an environmental or occupational illness.

questions.stem: In medical science, the term AETIOLOGY specifically refers to:

options.option_text: the study of the causes and origins of diseases
the process of patient recovery after a serious illness
the branch of medicine concerned with surgical operations
the scientific system of classifying and naming diseases

questions.explanation: A is correct: aetiology (also spelled etiology) is the branch of medicine that investigates the causes and risk factors underlying diseases — for instance, tobacco smoking is the aetiology of lung cancer. Option B describes rehabilitation or convalescence. Option C describes surgery. Option D describes nosology (disease classification), a common distractor because it sounds closely related.

questions.stem: An IATROGENIC condition in clinical medicine is one that is:

options.option_text: caused or worsened as a direct result of medical treatment
inherited genetically and passed down from a parent
arising from an untreated bacterial infection over time
resulting from chronic poor diet and nutritional deficiency

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'iatrogenic' derives from Greek 'iatros' (physician) + 'genesis' (origin), literally meaning 'physician-caused'. Drug-induced kidney injury from a prescribed medication is a textbook iatrogenic condition. Option B describes a hereditary or congenital condition. Option C describes a complication of neglect, not treatment. Option D describes a nutritional disorder — none of these imply a treatment-origin.

questions.stem: In oncology, a patient is said to be in REMISSION when which of the following occurs?

options.option_text: signs and symptoms of the cancer decrease or disappear entirely
cancer cells begin to spread aggressively to distant organs
the body develops resistance to chemotherapy drugs over time
the original tumour recurs at its primary site after treatment

questions.explanation: A is correct: remission (partial or complete) means measurable reduction or absence of cancer signs — it does not mean cure. Option B describes metastasis, the opposite of remission. Option C describes chemotherapy resistance, a separate clinical problem. Option D describes relapse or recurrence, which is the antonym of remission. Candidates frequently confuse remission with cure or conflate it with relapse.

questions.stem: Which statement CORRECTLY distinguishes MORBIDITY from MORTALITY in public health statistics?

options.option_text: Morbidity refers to disease incidence rates; mortality refers to death rates
Morbidity tracks recovery outcomes; mortality tracks new infection cases
Morbidity applies only to mental illness; mortality applies to physical disease
Both terms measure death rates but differ in the target age demographic

questions.explanation: A is correct: morbidity rate measures how many people in a population are affected by a disease (prevalence/incidence), while mortality rate measures the number of deaths from that disease. Option B reverses and distorts both definitions. Option C is false — morbidity covers all diseases, not only mental illness. Option D is the most tempting trap: both words superficially sound like they relate to death ('morbid' = gloomy), but morbidity is about illness, not death.
